public_rationale: The forecast is supported on the ordinary existence reading. IIHS independently found that deployed Waymo vehicles had lower overall and injury-crash rates than human drivers across comparable areas and years, with roughly 50 million driverless miles studied. This establishes sustained driverless operation with a safety advantage within defined operating areas. It does not establish universal, all-conditions autonomy.
limitations: The result depends on allowing operation within defined service areas.
Human and automated-vehicle reporting practices differ; IIHS used judgment to identify comparable crashes.
The aggregate advantage was not present in every city's point estimate.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Reliable self-driving cars will emerge and will eventually be safer than human drivers.

statement.excerpt: I do still think that reliable self-driving cars will emerge, and eventually be safer than humans, who can get distracted, become tired and so forth.
statement.document_title: Why driverless cars might—or might not—be at the end of the road

our_interpretation: This is an existence forecast, with no fixed deadline.
The plain reading includes genuinely driverless vehicles operating reliably within defined service areas. It does not require every vehicle to drive everywhere under every condition.
Reliable means sustained real-world operation without a human supervising the driving. Safer means lower crash and injury-crash rates per mile against reasonably comparable human driving.
criteria.support_condition: Independent real-world evidence establishes sustained driverless operation and lower overall and injury-crash rates than comparable human drivers within the vehicles' operating areas.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A decisive finding establishes that such vehicles cannot emerge. Failures of particular systems or the passage of time alone cannot contradict an unlimited eventual forecast.

evidence.explanation: The study compares driverless operation with human driving in matching areas and years, adjusting for reporting differences. The event date marks the final year of the 2021–2024 study period; this is an aggregate finding, not a 2024-only rate.

evidence.locator: Results paragraph beginning with Waymo's approximately 50 million driverless miles
evidence.explanation: The same study documents roughly 50 million driverless miles and a lower injury-crash rate, supporting sustained deployment and the safety comparison. Results varied by city: Austin's small sample had a 4% higher overall rate, and IIHS limits its conclusion to the operations studied.

conclusive_event.meets_rule: The independent study, publicly reported on July 23, 2026, documents sustained driverless deployment through 2024 and lower comparable crash rates. Its injury-crash result and mileage exposure are documented in e2.
